Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning

Zhuguanyu Wu1,2 Congjia Chen111footnotemark: 1  Ruihao Gong1,2 Yang Yong2 Shiqiao Gu2 Yi Xu1 Xianglong Liu1 1Beihang University 2Sensetime Research ††thanks: Equal Contribution.††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to post-train diffusion and flow models for visual generation, improving visual quality and prompt alignment through reward feedback (Black et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). A common formulation treats denoising as a sequence of decisions, with intermediate latents as states and rewards assigned to generated samples. For deterministic flow samplers, Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO introduce stochastic transitions to support exploration and likelihood-ratio optimization (Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025). Meanwhile, distillation compresses generation into a few denoising steps (Yin et al., 2024; Contributors, 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026), motivating RL methods that retain this efficient inference schedule. Each transition then spans a wide interval of noise levels, making the finite-step stochastic policy an important design choice.

Large transitions expose differences between stochastic constructions. The standard Euler–Maruyama transition used by Flow-GRPO generally does not satisfy Flow-CPS’s coefficient-preserving constraint (Liu et al., 2025; Wang and Yu, 2025). Flow-CPS enforces this constraint by constructing transitions directly at the target noise level (Wang and Yu, 2025). We adopt the same constraint, which fixes the sum of the squared noise coefficients while allowing different splits between predicted noise carried over from the current state and fresh Gaussian noise. Flow-CPS specifies this split through a single normalized stochasticity parameter shared across timesteps and tuned empirically. The constraint thus defines an admissible family but leaves a policy-selection question: which transition should serve as the training policy?

To answer this question, we introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), motivated by the distinction between the distributions used for policy optimization and the velocity predictions used for generation. GRPO moderates updates through likelihood-ratio clipping and reference-policy regularization, both defined on stochastic transition distributions, whereas deterministic inference depends on velocity predictions. Within the coefficient-preserving isotropic Gaussian family, the same velocity-output update can induce different changes in the transition distribution depending on the noise split. We therefore propose the following selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update.

To characterize this criterion, we identify a scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for a prescribed velocity-output update. Its square quantifies policy sensitivity, measuring how strongly the stochastic transition distribution responds to changes in the velocity prediction. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional log-likelihood-ratio variance under the old policy. This characterization holds for finite updates and yields the same minimizing coefficients for all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, before reward-based optimization determines which updates to take.

The resulting problem has a unique closed-form solution, with coefficients determined by both source and target noise levels. Under rectified-flow parameterization, it recovers the one-step SDE-DPM-Solver++ transition (Lu et al., 2022), providing a geometric optimality characterization of an existing sampling rule. At a fixed target noise level, the minimized geometry factor increases with the transition span, so larger transitions remain more sensitive to the same velocity update even under the optimal split. To account for the remaining variation across timesteps, we follow the gradient-scale matching principle of Team et al. (2025) to derive policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature.

We evaluate Geo-FSRL on four-step distilled Qwen-Image (Wu et al., 2025; Contributors, 2025) and Wan2.1 (Wan et al., 2025) models for image and video generation. It attains higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS in the main comparisons while retaining the original deterministic inference schedule.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose selecting stochastic policies by minimizing conditional KL for a given nonzero velocity-output update, reducing the problem to scalar optimization within a coefficient-preserving isotropic Gaussian family.

  • •

    We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, and characterize how the minimum geometry factor depends on the transition span at a fixed target noise level.

  • •

    We develop Geo-FSRL by combining the selected transition with closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights from gradient-scale matching, and demonstrate higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on four-step image and video models.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Flow Matching and GRPO

We consider rectified-flow models defined by the linear probability path

𝒙t=(1−t)​𝒙0+t​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰),t∈[0,1].\bm{x}_{t}=(1-t)\bm{x}_{0}+t\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}),\qquad t\in[0,1]. (1)

where 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} is a clean sample and the model 𝒗θ​(𝒙t,t)\bm{v}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t) is trained to predict the velocity 𝒗=ϵ−𝒙0\bm{v}=\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{x}_{0}. Given a prediction, the clean sample and the noise are estimated as

𝒙^0=𝒙t−t​𝒗θ​(𝒙t,t),ϵ^=𝒙t+(1−t)​𝒗θ​(𝒙t,t).\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{t}-t\bm{v}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t),\qquad\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}=\bm{x}_{t}+(1-t)\bm{v}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t). (2)

Sampling follows a decreasing timestep schedule 𝒯={t0=1>t1>⋯>tK=0}\mathcal{T}=\{t_{0}=1>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{K}=0\} with KK denoising steps; for a transition between timesteps t>st>s we write Δt,s=t−s>0\Delta_{t,s}=t-s>0 for its span.

For online RL, denoising is cast as a sequential decision process (Black et al., 2024): for the transition from tt to ss, the state is the prompt 𝒄\bm{c} together with the current latent 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, and the next latent 𝒙s\bm{x}_{s} is an action drawn from a stochastic policy qθ​(𝒙s∣𝒙t,𝒄)q_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c}). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) optimizes θ\theta without a learned value function. For each prompt, a group of MM trajectories is sampled from the current policy θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, which is frozen for one iteration, and the terminal rewards are converted into group-relative advantages AA. The reward-wise normalization and multi-reward combination used in our experiments are specified in Appendix B. With the policy ratio rt,s​(θ)=qθ​(𝒙s∣𝒙t,𝒄)/qθold​(𝒙s∣𝒙t,𝒄)r_{t,s}(\theta)=q_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c})/q_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c}), a standard reference-regularized objective is

ℒGRPO=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}={} −𝔼⁡[min⁡(rt,s​(θ)​A,clip⁡(rt,s​(θ),1−εclip,1+εclip)​A)]\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\left[\min\left(r_{t,s}(\theta)A,\,\operatorname{clip}\left(r_{t,s}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\right)A\right)\right] (3)
+λKL𝔼[DKL(qθ(⋅∣𝒙t,𝒄)∥qref(⋅∣𝒙t,𝒄))],\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\,\mathbb{E}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c})\,\|\,q_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c})\right)\right],

where expectations run over prompts and group trajectories, and qrefq_{\mathrm{ref}} is a frozen reference policy, typically the initial model. The sampling policy θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}} defines the ratio and is refreshed every iteration; qrefq_{\mathrm{ref}} anchors training. Section 3 analyzes the divergence between qθoldq_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} and qθq_{\theta} induced by one update, while the reference KL in Eq. 3 regularizes training.

2.2 Stochastic Transitions for Few-Step Flow RL

Flow matching ordinarily generates samples through a deterministic ODE. Substituting Eq. 2, the Euler update from tt to ss can be rewritten as 𝒙t−Δt,s​𝒗θ​(𝒙t,t)=(1−s)​𝒙^0+s​ϵ^\bm{x}_{t}-\Delta_{t,s}\bm{v}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t)=(1-s)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}+s\hat{\bm{\epsilon}} (Appendix A.1). Stochastic transitions used in flow RL inject Gaussian noise into this update, and those considered in this paper can all be written in the common form

𝒙s=(1−s)​𝒙^0+βt,s​ϵ^+αt,s​𝝃,𝝃∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰),\bm{x}_{s}=(1-s)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}+\beta_{t,s}\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}+\alpha_{t,s}\bm{\xi},\qquad\bm{\xi}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}), (4)

with 𝝃\bm{\xi} sampled independently; βt,s\beta_{t,s} scales the predicted noise and αt,s\alpha_{t,s} the newly injected noise. Appendix A.1 compares these coefficients in Table 5 and gives the derivations and implementation variants.

Flow-GRPO.

Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) constructs a continuous-time SDE whose marginals coincide with those of the flow ODE and discretizes each transition with Euler–Maruyama, using σt=a​t/(1−t)\sigma_{t}=a\sqrt{t/(1-t)} with a global noise level a>0a>0. For the standard uncapped construction at interior timesteps, the clean-sample coefficient remains 1−s1-s, while αt,s2+βt,s2−s2\alpha_{t,s}^{2}+\beta_{t,s}^{2}-s^{2} is strictly positive and grows quadratically with the span at fixed tt and σt\sigma_{t} (Table 5). These are algebraic properties of the transition coefficients; they do not by themselves determine the sample marginals under learned predictions or establish a performance disadvantage. Appendix A.1 treats the schedule endpoint and noise cap.

Flow-CPS.

Flow-CPS (Wang and Yu, 2025) instead constructs the transition directly at the target noise level, parameterizing the noise split by a global normalized stochasticity parameter ϕ∈(0,1]\phi\in(0,1], corresponding to an angle π​ϕ/2\pi\phi/2:

αt,s=s​sin⁡(π​ϕ/2),βt,s=s​cos⁡(π​ϕ/2).\alpha_{t,s}=s\sin(\pi\phi/2),\qquad\beta_{t,s}=s\cos(\pi\phi/2). (5)

These coefficients satisfy αt,s2+βt,s2=s2\alpha_{t,s}^{2}+\beta_{t,s}^{2}=s^{2} for every span, with the ODE Euler update at the deterministic boundary ϕ=0\phi=0. The constraint leaves a one-parameter family of (αt,s,βt,s)(\alpha_{t,s},\beta_{t,s}): every admissible ϕ\phi preserves the coefficients, and Flow-CPS selects ϕ\phi empirically. Section 3 optimizes this choice.

3 Geo-FSRL

Geo-FSRL selects a stochastic training policy by minimizing the conditional KL divergence induced by a prescribed nonzero velocity-output update. We first formulate this criterion, then derive an equivalent scalar optimization and its closed-form solution. Matched weights subsequently normalize explicit policy-gradient and reference-regularization scales without changing the selected policy’s likelihood ratios.

3.1 Admissible Stochastic Policies

For a transition with 0<s<t≤10<s<t\leq 1, we use the common form in Eq. 4 and impose

αt,s>0,0≤βt,s<s,αt,s2+βt,s2=s2.\alpha_{t,s}>0,\qquad 0\leq\beta_{t,s}<s,\qquad\alpha_{t,s}^{2}+\beta_{t,s}^{2}=s^{2}. (6)

Thus βt,s\beta_{t,s} indexes the policies, with αt,s=s2−βt,s2\alpha_{t,s}=\sqrt{s^{2}-\beta_{t,s}^{2}}. Fixing the total noise coefficient prevents trivially reducing conditional KL by injecting unbounded noise. Under oracle reconstruction, the predicted and fresh noise are independent standard Gaussians, reproducing the linear path’s noise coefficient at ss. Our conditional analysis requires only Gaussian fresh noise 𝝃\bm{\xi}; the learned noise prediction need not be standard Gaussian.

Substituting the reconstruction estimates into the transition gives

qβ(⋅∣𝒗)\displaystyle q_{\beta}(\cdot\mid\bm{v}) =𝒩⁡(𝝁β​(𝒗),αt,s2​𝑰),\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v}),\alpha_{t,s}^{2}\bm{I}\right), (7)
𝝁β​(𝒗)\displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v}) =(1−s+βt,s)𝒙t+κt,s𝒗,κt,s=−t(1−s)+(1−t)βt,s.\displaystyle=(1-s+\beta_{t,s})\bm{x}_{t}+\kappa_{t,s}\bm{v},\qquad\kappa_{t,s}=-t(1-s)+(1-t)\beta_{t,s}.

Fix a state (𝒙t,𝒄)(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c}) and timestep pair (t,s)(t,s). Let 𝒗0\bm{v}_{0} be the old velocity prediction and Δ​𝒗=𝒗θ−𝒗0∈ℝD\Delta\bm{v}=\bm{v}_{\theta}-\bm{v}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} an output update, where DD is the latent dimension. Each candidate β\beta keeps its coefficients and covariance fixed between old and updated policies; across candidates, we prescribe the same Δ​𝒗\Delta\bm{v} independently of the optimizer.

3.2 Policy Selection by Conditional KL

A common measure of model change.

The velocity output provides a common measure of model change across stochastic constructions. At the fixed state, the deterministic Euler update changes by −(t−s)​Δ​𝒗-(t-s)\Delta\bm{v}, independently of the training noise split. Yet the same Δ​𝒗\Delta\bm{v} can change stochastic transition distributions differently. Coefficient selection therefore determines how a model-output change is expressed in its training policy.

We seek to limit this distribution change for a prescribed output update. Within our Gaussian family, smaller conditional KL implies lower conditional log-ratio variance under each candidate’s old policy and, under the threshold condition in Section 3.4, a lower probability of leaving the clipping window. Loss reweighting can normalize explicit gradient and reference-penalty scales but leaves likelihood ratios for a prescribed output update unchanged, so these differences persist after scale matching.

Policy-selection criterion.

For each candidate, we measure the distribution change induced by an output update using the conditional KL divergence between its updated and old policies:

Kβ(Δ𝒗)=DKL(qβ(⋅∣𝒗0+Δ𝒗)∥qβ(⋅∣𝒗0)).K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{\beta}(\cdot\mid\bm{v}_{0}+\Delta\bm{v})\,\|\,q_{\beta}(\cdot\mid\bm{v}_{0})\right). (8)

Our selection principle is to choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by the same prescribed nonzero velocity-output update. At fixed (𝒙t,𝒄,t,s)(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c},t,s) and Δ​𝒗≠𝟎\Delta\bm{v}\neq\bm{0}, this defines the optimization problem

min0≤βt,s<s⁡Kβ​(Δ​𝒗).\min_{0\leq\beta_{t,s}<s}\;K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v}). (9)

The criterion selects a policy for a prescribed update; reward feedback determines which output updates are useful. We next solve this conditional KL problem within the admissible family.

Gt,s​(βt,s)=|κt,s|αt,s=t⁡(1−s)−(1−t)​βt,ss2−βt,s2.G_{t,s}(\beta_{t,s})=\frac{|\kappa_{t,s}|}{\alpha_{t,s}}=\frac{t(1-s)-(1-t)\beta_{t,s}}{\sqrt{s^{2}-\beta_{t,s}^{2}}}. (10)

3.4 Geometry-Matched GRPO Training

Transition-wise weights.

The geometry factor also enters the explicit score scale and reference-KL curvature. We normalize these using the gradient-scale matching principle of Team et al. (2025). At a fixed action, the velocity-output score is

∇𝒗​log​qθ=κt,s⋆αt,s⋆​𝝃θ,𝝃θ=𝒙s−𝝁θ,t,sαt,s⋆.\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\theta}=\frac{\kappa_{t,s}^{\star}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{\star}}\bm{\xi}_{\theta},\qquad\bm{\xi}_{\theta}=\frac{\bm{x}_{s}-\bm{\mu}_{\theta,t,s}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{\star}}. (16)

The explicit coefficient has magnitude Gt,s⋆G_{t,s}^{\star}. The current and reference policies use the same coefficients and covariance, so their conditional KL has velocity-space curvature (Gt,s⋆)2​𝑰(G_{t,s}^{\star})^{2}\bm{I}. These factors vary across timestep pairs even after coefficient selection. We therefore use

wt,spolicy=cgeoGt,s⋆,wt,sKL=(cgeoGt,s⋆)2,w_{t,s}^{\mathrm{policy}}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{geo}}}{G_{t,s}^{\star}},\qquad w_{t,s}^{\mathrm{KL}}=\left(\frac{c_{\mathrm{geo}}}{G_{t,s}^{\star}}\right)^{2}, (17)

where cgeo>0c_{\mathrm{geo}}>0 is shared across transitions and the weights are constant with respect to model parameters. The derivation is given in Appendix A.4.

Training objective.

Following Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), we average log-densities over the DD scalar elements of the transition latent, i.e., all non-batch dimensions. Thus the clipped term uses r¯t,s=rt,s1/D\bar{r}_{t,s}=r_{t,s}^{1/D} and the reference regularizer uses D¯KL=DKL/D\overline{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}/D:

ℒgeo=𝔼[wt,spolicyℓ¯t,sclip(θ)+λKLwt,sKLD¯KL(qθ∥qref)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w_{t,s}^{\mathrm{policy}}\bar{\ell}_{t,s}^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}w_{t,s}^{\mathrm{KL}}\overline{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\theta}\,\|\,q_{\mathrm{ref}})\right]. (18)

Here ℓ¯clip\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{clip}} is the negative clipped surrogate in Eq. 3, with rr replaced by r¯\bar{r}, and both policies are conditioned on the recorded state. At fixed DD, dimension averaging changes the KL scale but leaves the minimizing coefficients and the relative 1/G⋆1/G^{\star} and 1/(G⋆)21/(G^{\star})^{2} weights unchanged. Advantage processing and hyperparameters are specified in Appendix B.

Policy sensitivity after scale matching.

For any candidate policy, applying its matched weight to the dimension-averaged velocity score at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}} gives −cgeo𝝃old/D-c_{\mathrm{geo}}\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{old}}/D. The weighted reference KL is cgeo2​‖𝒗θ−𝒗ref‖22/(2​D)c_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}\|\bm{v}_{\theta}-\bm{v}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}/(2D), so its penalty for a fixed velocity deviation is also identical across matched candidates. These cancellations normalize explicit loss scales. They do not change each candidate’s sampling distribution, likelihood ratio, or clipping thresholds.

For a prescribed output update at a fixed state, timestep pair, and dimension, let d=Gt,s​‖Δ​𝒗‖2d=G_{t,s}\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}. With an action drawn from the candidate’s old policy, the dimension-averaged log-ratio satisfies

log⁡r¯∼𝒩⁡(−d22​D,d2D2).\log\bar{r}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(-\frac{d^{2}}{2D},\frac{d^{2}}{D^{2}}\right). (19)

Thus minimizing Gt,sG_{t,s} still minimizes the conditional KL and log-ratio variance induced by the same output update after matching. It also minimizes the probability that r¯\bar{r} lies outside [1−εclip,1+εclip][1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}] whenever −log⁡(1−εclip)≤3​log⁡(1+εclip)-\log(1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})\leq 3\log(1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}), as holds for our εclip=10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}=10^{-3} (Proposition 2, Appendix A.2.4). This gives a direct connection between coefficient selection and the clipping window used in training.

This probability compares prescribed updates under the respective old-policy distributions. Actual updates also depend on sampled advantages, residuals, model Jacobians, and the optimizer, while active clipping additionally depends on the advantage sign. Scale matching therefore does not guarantee identical realized updates or a lower observed clipping frequency. For a recorded action reused after an update, 𝝃θ=𝝃old−(κt,s/αt,s)​Δ​𝒗\bm{\xi}_{\theta}=\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{old}}-(\kappa_{t,s}/\alpha_{t,s})\Delta\bm{v}; the resulting dependence of later gradients on the coefficients is detailed in Appendix A.4.

Effect on the sampling distribution.

At the same state and velocity prediction, changing the coefficients generally changes both the conditional mean and fresh-noise variance: 𝝁β2−𝝁β1=(β2−β1)​ϵ^\bm{\mu}_{\beta_{2}}-\bm{\mu}_{\beta_{1}}=(\beta_{2}-\beta_{1})\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}. A global learning-rate or clipping adjustment leaves this sampling distribution unchanged. Moreover, geometry-factor ratios generally vary across transitions. Coefficient selection therefore changes the policy beyond a uniform rescaling of its optimization steps.

The sampling and training procedure is given in Algorithm 1 (Appendix B.2).

4 Experiments

We evaluate four-step image and video generation with Geo-FSRL, Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), Flow-CPS (Wang and Yu, 2025), and a four-step DiffusionNFT adaptation (Zheng et al., 2026). GRPO-based comparisons share single-stochastic-transition rollouts. Flow-CPS and Geo-FSRL use gradient-scale matching with weights from their respective coefficients unless ablated. Both tasks use 4 sampling steps in training and evaluation. For each task, all reward curves and tabulated automatic scores use the same fixed validation set of 256 prompts, disjoint from training prompts. The horizontal axes count optimizer updates. Training uses 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs; hyperparameters, schedules, and reward normalization appear in Appendix B.

4.1 Few-Step Text-to-Image

Experimental Setup. We fine-tune all diffusion-transformer parameters of Qwen-Image-2512-Lightning-4steps11 1 Distilled checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/lightx2v/Qwen-Image-Lightning. (Wu et al., 2025; Contributors, 2025), distilled from the 20B MMDiT Qwen-Image, at 720 ×\times 720 resolution.

Reward Models. We optimize HPSv3 (Ma et al., 2025) for human preference, alone or jointly with CLIPScore (Radford et al., 2021) for image-text alignment.

Dataset. Prompts come from the text-to-image generation split of OpenGPT-4o-Image (Chen et al., 2025), a diverse corpus of about 40k prompts.

Single-reward Training Results. We compare Geo-FSRL with Flow-CPS at normalized stochasticity ϕ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0}\phi\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0\}, using each policy’s matched weights. Geo-FSRL derives coefficients from each timestep pair. It improves similarly to the best tested Flow-CPS setting, ϕ=0.7\phi=0.7, in early and middle training (Figure 1(a)), but finishes higher: 14.05 versus 13.90; Flow-GRPO reaches 13.62 (Table 1). Maximum injected noise, ϕ=1\phi=1, is included and differs from the geometry optimum at internal timesteps. The tested DiffusionNFT adaptation exhibits early reward deterioration and visible pixel noise; this observation is specific to that adaptation.

A global Flow-CPS ϕ\phi specifies one geometry factor per stochastic transition. Changing ϕ\phi can improve the factor at one transition while worsening it at another, whereas the closed-form schedule minimizes each separately. The scan therefore compares globally fixed noise splits with a transition-wise rule, rather than testing a monotonic relation between any single geometry factor and final reward.

Multi-reward Joint Training Results. Joint HPSv3 and CLIPScore training retains the best single-reward Flow-CPS setting, ϕ=0.7\phi=0.7. Geo-FSRL leads both final metrics (Figure 1(b,c), Table 1): 13.80 HPSv3 versus Flow-CPS’s 13.58, and 1.008 CLIPScore versus Flow-GRPO’s 0.996, absolute gains of 0.22 and 0.012 over the respective strongest baselines. Qualitative examples appear in Appendix D.

Human evaluation. Five evaluators blinded to method identity compare Geo-FSRL and Flow-CPS on 20 image pairs from randomly sampled prompts, with shared prompts and seeds and shuffled presentation order. Geo-FSRL receives 54% of Visual Quality votes (aesthetics) and 58% of Overall Preference votes (prompt adherence and visual appeal; Table 2). These percentages are descriptive results from a small evaluation.

Policy Reweighting Ablation. We vary policy weighting while retaining matched KL weighting for both Flow-CPS and our Geo-FSRL, ensuring consistent KL regularization strength across transitions. As shown in Table 3, policy weighting improves Flow-CPS by 0.21 and Geo-FSRL by 0.44. Geo-FSRL scores 0.08 below Flow-CPS without policy weighting and 0.15 above with their respective matched weights. The observed ordering therefore changes with policy weighting. These results support the combined design in this setting, evaluating coefficient selection together with its corresponding weights. Appendix C provides the validation curves and a controlled gradient-scale analysis.

4.2 Few-Step Text-to-Video

Experimental Setup. We distill Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (Wan et al., 2025) to four steps using DMD2 with the LightX2V training framework22 2 https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_train (Contributors, 2025). We then fine-tune all diffusion-transformer parameters, generating 81 frames at 832 ×\times 480 resolution.

Reward Models. We jointly optimize HPSv3-General and HPSv3-Percentile for frame-level visual quality and caption alignment, and VideoAlign-MQ for motion quality (Liu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2025); Appendix B specifies aggregation.

Dataset. Following Self-Forcing (Huang et al., 2026), we use prompts from LLM-extended VidProM (Wang and Yang, 2024).

Results. Geo-FSRL leads all three final metrics (Figure 2, Table 4), gaining 1.09 HPSv3-General, 0.80 HPSv3-Percentile, and 0.81 VideoAlign-MQ over the respective strongest baselines. Validation curves show a clearer advantage than for single-reward images. These results evaluate the complete method on a second modality; component comparisons remain in the image ablation. Selected video frames appear in Appendix D.

5 Related Work

Policy optimization for fast generation. DDPO and DPOK use policy gradients for stochastic denoising (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023). Their reference implementations use DDIM (η=1\eta=1) (Song et al., 2021), yielding ancestral posterior-variance transitions on the timestep grid; their formulations do not require this choice.33 3 Default settings: DDPO and DPOK. RLCM applies RL to few-step consistency models with Gaussian re-noising of endpoint predictions (Oertell et al., 2024); our setting retains the velocity parameterization of distilled flows.

Stochastic policies for flow RL. Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO apply group-relative optimization to stochastic flow trajectories (Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025). Flow-CPS demonstrates four-step training and evaluation with coefficient-preserving transitions (Wang and Yu, 2025). Within this family, our conditional KL criterion (Section 3.2) selects the existing first-order SDE-DPM-Solver++ transition (Lu et al., 2022). Our policy-gradient and KL weights specialize LongCat-Video’s gradient-scale matching principle (Team et al., 2025).

Allocation of stochasticity and computation. MixGRPO confines stochastic sampling and policy updates to a moving SDE window (Li et al., 2025); TempFlow-GRPO combines designated stochastic branching, noise-aware weighting, and seed grouping (He et al., 2026); BranchGRPO restructures rollouts (Li et al., 2026). Our rollout shares this mixed stochastic–deterministic structure; we address coefficient selection within a stochastic transition.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce Geo-FSRL, a closed-form stochastic policy selection rule with corresponding loss reweighting for few-step flow reinforcement learning. Within a coefficient-preserving isotropic Gaussian family, the selected policy minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any prescribed nonzero velocity-output update, with the same minimizing coefficients across update magnitudes and directions. This separates policy selection from scale matching, which normalizes explicit loss scales without changing likelihood ratios for a prescribed output update. In both four-step text-to-image and text-to-video experiments, Geo-FSRL achieves faster reward improvement and higher final validation scores than the compared baselines, while retaining the original deterministic solver at inference. These results support treating stochastic policy construction as an explicit design choice for few-step reinforcement learning and motivate further study of its interaction with reward objectives and optimization.

Appendix A Additional Derivations and Proofs

A.1 Coefficient Form of Finite Flow Transitions

This section derives the unified coefficient representation of Eq. 4 for the entries of Table 5, with emphasis on the standard Euler–Maruyama transition of Flow-GRPO and the modifications used in its implementation at the schedule endpoint and under a capped noise scale. The coefficients of Flow-CPS and of the policies studied in this paper are given directly in the main text. Throughout, 0<s<t<10<s<t<1 unless stated otherwise, Δt,s=t−s\Delta_{t,s}=t-s, and the estimates 𝒙^0=𝒙t−t​𝒗θ\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{t}-t\bm{v}_{\theta} and ϵ^=𝒙t+(1−t)​𝒗θ\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}=\bm{x}_{t}+(1-t)\bm{v}_{\theta} are evaluated at (𝒙t,t)(\bm{x}_{t},t); the arguments of 𝒗θ\bm{v}_{\theta} are omitted.

A.1.1 Deterministic Euler Step

Inverting the definitions of the estimates gives 𝒙t=(1−t)​𝒙^0+t​ϵ^\bm{x}_{t}=(1-t)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}+t\hat{\bm{\epsilon}} and 𝒗θ=ϵ^−𝒙^0\bm{v}_{\theta}=\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}-\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}. Hence,

𝒙t−Δt,s​𝒗θ=(1−t+Δt,s)​𝒙^0+(t−Δt,s)​ϵ^=(1−s)​𝒙^0+s​ϵ^,\bm{x}_{t}-\Delta_{t,s}\bm{v}_{\theta}=(1-t+\Delta_{t,s})\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}+(t-\Delta_{t,s})\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}=(1-s)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}+s\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}, (20)

which is the identity quoted in Section 2.2 and the ODE Euler row of Table 5. The identity holds for any velocity output and any span; it rewrites the Euler update in the coefficient form and makes no claim about the accuracy of the update as an ODE solution.

When this holds, the coefficient of the predicted noise changes sign. The condition is easier to satisfy for large spans and for source timesteps close to 11.

Implementation modifications.

The implementation of the Flow-GRPO transition differs from Eq. 22 only in the noise scale, which is replaced by an effective scale σ~t,s\tilde{\sigma}_{t,s} that accounts for the schedule endpoint and for an optional cap on the injected noise. Let

σt,sbase={a​t1−t,t<1,a1−s,t=1,σ~t,s=min⁡{σt,sbase,cclipΔt,s},\sigma_{t,s}^{\mathrm{base}}=\begin{cases}a\sqrt{\dfrac{t}{1-t}},&t<1,\\[5.16663pt] \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1-s}},&t=1,\end{cases}\qquad\tilde{\sigma}_{t,s}=\min\left\{\sigma_{t,s}^{\mathrm{base}},\,\frac{c_{\mathrm{clip}}}{\sqrt{\Delta_{t,s}}}\right\}, (28)

where cclip>0c_{\mathrm{clip}}>0 is the cap on the standard deviation of the injected noise, and cclip=∞c_{\mathrm{clip}}=\infty when no cap is used. The implemented update is Eq. 22 with σt\sigma_{t} replaced by σ~t,s\tilde{\sigma}_{t,s}, so Eqs. equation 24–equation 25 hold verbatim with the same substitution, and the injected noise has standard deviation αt,sE=σ~t,s​Δt,s≤cclip\alpha_{t,s}^{\mathrm{E}}=\tilde{\sigma}_{t,s}\sqrt{\Delta_{t,s}}\leq c_{\mathrm{clip}}. Two cases are worth recording explicitly.

First transition before capping. The base scale a​t/(1−t)a\sqrt{t/(1-t)} diverges as t→1t\rightarrow 1, so the interior formulas apply to t<1t<1 only; at t0=1t_{0}=1 the implementation replaces the source timestep by the target timestep inside the denominator 1−t1-t, i.e. it uses 1−s1-s in place of 1−t1-t, which gives the finite value σ1,sbase=a/1−s\sigma_{1,s}^{\mathrm{base}}=a/\sqrt{1-s} for s<1s<1. If the cap is inactive, substituting t=1t=1 and this scale into Eq. 24 yields

α1,sE=a,β1,sE=s−a22,(α1,sE)2+(β1,sE)2−s2=a2​(1−s)+a44,\alpha_{1,s}^{\mathrm{E}}=a,\qquad\beta_{1,s}^{\mathrm{E}}=s-\frac{a^{2}}{2},\qquad\left(\alpha_{1,s}^{\mathrm{E}}\right)^{2}+\left(\beta_{1,s}^{\mathrm{E}}\right)^{2}-s^{2}=a^{2}(1-s)+\frac{a^{4}}{4}, (29)

so the first transition injects noise with standard deviation aa irrespective of the span. With the cap, the cap threshold at t=1t=1 is cclip/1−sc_{\mathrm{clip}}/\sqrt{1-s}, which has the same denominator as the base scale, so α1,sE=min⁡{a,cclip}\alpha_{1,s}^{\mathrm{E}}=\min\{a,c_{\mathrm{clip}}\}.

Active cap. In the region where the cap is active, i.e. (σt,sbase)2​Δt,s>cclip2(\sigma_{t,s}^{\mathrm{base}})^{2}\Delta_{t,s}>c_{\mathrm{clip}}^{2}, the effective scale satisfies σ~t,s2=cclip2/Δt,s\tilde{\sigma}_{t,s}^{2}=c_{\mathrm{clip}}^{2}/\Delta_{t,s} and Eqs. equation 24–equation 25 become

αt,sE=cclip,βt,sE=s−cclip22​t,(αt,sE)2+(βt,sE)2−s2=cclip2​Δt,st+cclip44​t2.\alpha_{t,s}^{\mathrm{E}}=c_{\mathrm{clip}},\qquad\beta_{t,s}^{\mathrm{E}}=s-\frac{c_{\mathrm{clip}}^{2}}{2t},\qquad\left(\alpha_{t,s}^{\mathrm{E}}\right)^{2}+\left(\beta_{t,s}^{\mathrm{E}}\right)^{2}-s^{2}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{clip}}^{2}\Delta_{t,s}}{t}+\frac{c_{\mathrm{clip}}^{4}}{4t^{2}}. (30)

At fixed tt and cclipc_{\mathrm{clip}}, the deviation is therefore affine in the span inside the active region, and it remains strictly positive, so the capped transition still lies outside the coefficient-preserving family. Outside the active region the uncapped coefficients apply. Whether the cap is active for a given transition depends on the schedule, the noise level, and cclipc_{\mathrm{clip}}; the values used in our experiments are reported in Appendix B.

Terminal boundary.

At s=0s=0 the coefficient-preserving condition reduces to αt,0=βt,0=0\alpha_{t,0}=\beta_{t,0}=0, and relative deviations normalized by s2s^{2} are undefined; this is consistent with keeping the final transition deterministic.

A.2 Conditional KL and Likelihood-Ratio Geometry

A.2.1 KL Equivalence and Fisher Information

Proof of Proposition 1.

Fix (𝒙t,𝒄,t,s)(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{c},t,s) and one admissible coefficient choice. The old and updated policies have common covariance αt,s2​𝑰\alpha_{t,s}^{2}\bm{I}, and their mean difference is

Δ​𝝁=𝝁β​(𝒗0+Δ​𝒗)−𝝁β​(𝒗0)=κt,s​Δ​𝒗.\Delta\bm{\mu}=\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v}_{0}+\Delta\bm{v})-\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v}_{0})=\kappa_{t,s}\Delta\bm{v}. (31)

The equal-covariance Gaussian KL formula therefore gives, in either direction,

Kβ​(Δ​𝒗)=‖Δ​𝝁‖222​αt,s2=12​Gt,s2​‖Δ​𝒗‖22.K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v})=\frac{\|\Delta\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\alpha_{t,s}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}G_{t,s}^{2}\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}^{2}. (32)

This identity is exact for finite output differences. Moreover, t⁡(1−s)−(1−t)​βt,s≥t⁡(1−s)−(1−t)​s=t−s>0t(1-s)-(1-t)\beta_{t,s}\geq t(1-s)-(1-t)s=t-s>0, so Gt,s>0G_{t,s}>0 throughout the family. For any prescribed nonzero update, ‖Δ​𝒗‖22/2\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}^{2}/2 is a positive constant across candidates. Minimizing the conditional KL in Eq. 9 is therefore equivalent to minimizing Gt,s2G_{t,s}^{2} or Gt,sG_{t,s}, which establishes Eq. 12. For two candidates A,BA,B, Eq. 32 also implies GA≤GBG_{A}\leq G_{B} if and only if KA​(Δ​𝒗)≤KB​(Δ​𝒗)K_{A}(\Delta\bm{v})\leq K_{B}(\Delta\bm{v}) for every output update; the reverse implication follows by evaluating any nonzero update. The minimizing coefficients are consequently independent of the prescribed update’s nonzero magnitude and direction. □\square

Normalized KL response and Fisher information.

Dividing Eq. 32 by ‖Δ​𝒗‖22/2\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}^{2}/2 for a nonzero update gives the normalized KL response Gt,s2G_{t,s}^{2}, interpreted as policy sensitivity in Eq. 14. To obtain the Fisher information, differentiate with the action 𝒙s\bm{x}_{s} held fixed:

∇𝒗​log​qβ​(𝒙s∣𝒗)=κt,sαt,s2​(𝒙s−𝝁β​(𝒗)).\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\beta}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{v})=\frac{\kappa_{t,s}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{2}}(\bm{x}_{s}-\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v})). (33)

Under the policy at 𝒗\bm{v}, write 𝒙s−𝝁β​(𝒗)=αt,s​𝝃\bm{x}_{s}-\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v})=\alpha_{t,s}\bm{\xi} with 𝝃∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰)\bm{\xi}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}). Hence

ℐ𝒗=𝔼⁡[(∇𝒗​log​qβ)​(∇𝒗​log​qβ)⊤]=κt,s2αt,s2​𝑰=Gt,s2​𝑰.\mathcal{I}_{\bm{v}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\beta})(\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\beta})^{\top}\right]=\frac{\kappa_{t,s}^{2}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{2}}\bm{I}=G_{t,s}^{2}\bm{I}. (34)

A.2.2 Likelihood-Ratio Moments

Keep the state and timestep pair fixed, and prescribe an output update Δ​𝒗∈ℝD\Delta\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} independently of the action used to evaluate the ratio. For an action from the old policy, write 𝒙s=𝝁β​(𝒗0)+αt,s​𝝃\bm{x}_{s}=\bm{\mu}_{\beta}(\bm{v}_{0})+\alpha_{t,s}\bm{\xi}, 𝝃∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰)\bm{\xi}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}), and set 𝒛=κt,s​Δ​𝒗/αt,s\bm{z}=\kappa_{t,s}\Delta\bm{v}/\alpha_{t,s}. For r=qβ​(𝒙s∣𝒗0+Δ​𝒗)/qβ​(𝒙s∣𝒗0)r=q_{\beta}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{v}_{0}+\Delta\bm{v})/q_{\beta}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{v}_{0}), the Gaussian log-density difference is

log⁡r\displaystyle\log r =−‖αt,s​𝝃−κt,s​Δ​𝒗‖22−‖αt,s​𝝃‖222​αt,s2\displaystyle=-\frac{\|\alpha_{t,s}\bm{\xi}-\kappa_{t,s}\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\alpha_{t,s}\bm{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\alpha_{t,s}^{2}} (35)
=𝝃⊤𝒛−12∥𝒛∥22,∥𝒛∥2=Gt,s∥Δ𝒗∥2=d.\displaystyle=\bm{\xi}^{\top}\bm{z}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{z}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\|\bm{z}\|_{2}=G_{t,s}\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}=d.

Since 𝝃⊤​𝒛∼𝒩⁡(0,d2)\bm{\xi}^{\top}\bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,d^{2}),

logr∼𝒩(−d2/2,d2),Var(logr)=2Kβ(Δ𝒗).\log r\sim\mathcal{N}(-d^{2}/2,d^{2}),\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\log r)=2K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v}). (36)

In particular, −𝔼qold[logr]=d2/2=DKL(qold∥qθ)=Kβ(Δ𝒗)-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\mathrm{old}}}[\log r]=d^{2}/2=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\mathrm{old}}\|q_{\theta})=K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v}), where the last equality uses the common covariance. The log-normal moments are

𝔼qold​[rm]=exp⁡(m2−m2​d2),𝔼⁡[r]=1,Var⁡(r)=ed2−1.\mathbb{E}_{q_{\mathrm{old}}}[r^{m}]=\exp\!\left(\frac{m^{2}-m}{2}d^{2}\right),\qquad\mathbb{E}[r]=1,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(r)=e^{d^{2}}-1. (37)

These conditional moments characterize likelihood changes without assumptions on rewards or advantages.

A.2.3 Dimension-Averaged Log-Densities

The implemented ratio is r¯=exp⁡((log⁡qθ−log⁡qold)/D)=r1/D\bar{r}=\exp((\log q_{\theta}-\log q_{\mathrm{old}})/D)=r^{1/D}, where D≥1D\geq 1 is the latent dimension. Under the same fixed-state, prescribed-update comparison, Eq. 36 gives

log⁡r¯∼𝒩⁡(−d22​D,d2D2),K¯β=KβD=Gt,s22​D​‖Δ​𝒗‖22.\log\bar{r}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(-\frac{d^{2}}{2D},\frac{d^{2}}{D^{2}}\right),\qquad\overline{K}_{\beta}=\frac{K_{\beta}}{D}=\frac{G_{t,s}^{2}}{2D}\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}^{2}. (38)

Consequently, Var⁡(log⁡r¯)=2​K¯β/D\operatorname{Var}(\log\bar{r})=2\overline{K}_{\beta}/D. With DD fixed across candidate coefficients, minimizing Gt,sG_{t,s} minimizes both the normalized KL and the averaged log-ratio variance for the same output update.

The quantity r¯\bar{r} is a scaled surrogate, not generally the density ratio of the two policies. Its moments are

𝔼⁡[r¯]=exp⁡(−d22​D+d22​D2),Var⁡(r¯)=exp⁡(−d2D+d2D2)​(exp⁡(d2D2)−1).\mathbb{E}[\bar{r}]=\exp\!\left(-\frac{d^{2}}{2D}+\frac{d^{2}}{2D^{2}}\right),\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\bar{r})=\exp\!\left(-\frac{d^{2}}{D}+\frac{d^{2}}{D^{2}}\right)\left(\exp\!\left(\frac{d^{2}}{D^{2}}\right)-1\right). (39)

For D>2D>2 this variance is not globally monotone in d2d^{2} and tends to zero as d2→∞d^{2}\to\infty. The KL and log-ratio variance ordering therefore does not imply a global ordering of Var⁡(r¯)\operatorname{Var}(\bar{r}).

A.2.4 Clipping-Window Exceedance

Proposition 2 (Population clipping-window exceedance)

Fix the state, timestep pair, and dimension D≥1D\geq 1, and prescribe Δ​𝐯\Delta\bm{v} independently of the evaluation draw from each candidate’s old policy. Let 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, d=Gt,s​‖Δ​𝐯‖2d=G_{t,s}\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}, and

a=−D​log⁡(1−ϵ),b=D​log⁡(1+ϵ).a=-D\log(1-\epsilon),\qquad b=D\log(1+\epsilon). (40)

For d>0d>0, the probability of leaving the clipping window is

pout​(d)\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{out}}(d) :=Pr⁡(r¯∉[1−ϵ,1+ϵ])\displaystyle:=\Pr\!\left(\bar{r}\notin[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]\right) (41)
=Φ⁡(d2−ad)+Φ⁡(−d2−bd),\displaystyle=\Phi\!\left(\frac{d}{2}-\frac{a}{d}\right)+\Phi\!\left(-\frac{d}{2}-\frac{b}{d}\right),

where Φ\Phi is the standard normal distribution function, and pout​(0)=0p_{\mathrm{out}}(0)=0. If a≤3​ba\leq 3b, then pout​(d)p_{\mathrm{out}}(d) is strictly increasing for d>0d>0. Hence, under this condition, minimizing Gt,sG_{t,s} also minimizes the population clipping-window exceedance probability for every prescribed nonzero output update.

Proof.

By Eq. 38, logr¯=(−d2/2+dZ)/D\log\bar{r}=(-d^{2}/2+dZ)/D with Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). The lower-window event is Z<d/2−a/dZ<d/2-a/d, and the upper-window event is Z>d/2+b/dZ>d/2+b/d, which gives Eq. 41. At d=0d=0, r¯=1\bar{r}=1 almost surely.

Let φ\varphi denote the standard normal density. Differentiating for d>0d>0 gives

pout′​(d)=φ⁡(d2−ad)​(12+ad2)+φ⁡(d2+bd)​(−12+bd2).p_{\mathrm{out}}^{\prime}(d)=\varphi\!\left(\frac{d}{2}-\frac{a}{d}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{a}{d^{2}}\right)+\varphi\!\left(\frac{d}{2}+\frac{b}{d}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{b}{d^{2}}\right). (42)

If d2≤2​bd^{2}\leq 2b, the first term is positive and the second is nonnegative. If d2>2​bd^{2}>2b, use a>b>0a>b>0 and a≤3​ba\leq 3b to obtain

φ⁡(d/2−a/d)φ⁡(d/2+b/d)=exp⁡(a+b2−a2−b22​d2)≥exp⁡((a+b)​(3​b−a)4​b)≥1.\frac{\varphi(d/2-a/d)}{\varphi(d/2+b/d)}=\exp\!\left(\frac{a+b}{2}-\frac{a^{2}-b^{2}}{2d^{2}}\right)\geq\exp\!\left(\frac{(a+b)(3b-a)}{4b}\right)\geq 1. (43)

Substitution into Eq. 42 then yields pout′​(d)≥φ⁡(d/2+b/d)​(a+b)/d2>0p_{\mathrm{out}}^{\prime}(d)\geq\varphi(d/2+b/d)(a+b)/d^{2}>0. This proves strict monotonicity. □\square

The condition a≤3​ba\leq 3b is equivalent to −log⁡(1−ϵ)≤3​log⁡(1+ϵ)-\log(1-\epsilon)\leq 3\log(1+\epsilon) and holds for the experimental choice ϵ=0.001\epsilon=0.001, independently of DD. The proposition orders the total population probability of leaving the window. Active PPO clipping additionally depends on the advantage sign: the clipped branch is active above the upper threshold for positive advantages and below the lower threshold for negative advantages. The result also does not establish an ordering of empirical minibatch fractions when the output update depends on the same samples used to evaluate those fractions.

A.2.5 Fisher Metric in Parameter Space

Let 𝑱θ=∂𝒗θ/∂θ\bm{J}_{\theta}=\partial\bm{v}_{\theta}/\partial\theta at the fixed conditioning state. The chain rule gives

∇θ​log​qθ=𝑱θ⊤​∇𝒗​log​qθ,ℐθ=𝑱θ⊤​ℐ𝒗​𝑱θ=Gt,s2​𝑱θ⊤​𝑱θ.\nabla_{\theta}\log q_{\theta}=\bm{J}_{\theta}^{\top}\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\theta},\qquad\mathcal{I}_{\theta}=\bm{J}_{\theta}^{\top}\mathcal{I}_{\bm{v}}\bm{J}_{\theta}=G_{t,s}^{2}\bm{J}_{\theta}^{\top}\bm{J}_{\theta}. (44)

For the same model and state, coefficient selection changes the scalar factor multiplying this conditional metric. It does not change the Jacobian or its directional anisotropy. Unlike the exact KL identity in output space, the corresponding quadratic approximation in parameter space uses a local linearization of the model. A shared parameter update need not independently realize prescribed output changes across states.

A.2.6 Equivalent KL-Budget Interpretation

The same conditional comparison can be expressed as an output-space allowance. For a common budget δ>0\delta>0, define 𝒯β​(δ)={Δ​𝒗∈ℝD:Kβ​(Δ​𝒗)≤δ}\mathcal{T}_{\beta}(\delta)=\{\Delta\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}:K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v})\leq\delta\}. Equation 32 gives

Kβ(Δ𝒗)≤δ⟺∥Δ𝒗∥2≤2​δGt,s.K_{\beta}(\Delta\bm{v})\leq\delta\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\|\Delta\bm{v}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{2\delta}}{G_{t,s}}. (45)

Thus the admissible region is an entire centered ball with radius

ρβ​(δ)=2​δGt,s​(βt,s).\rho_{\beta}(\delta)=\frac{\sqrt{2\delta}}{G_{t,s}(\beta_{t,s})}. (46)

Comparing these concentric balls yields

GA≤GB⟺𝒯B(δ)⊆𝒯A(δ)for every δ>0.G_{A}\leq G_{B}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{T}_{B}(\delta)\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{A}(\delta)\quad\text{for every }\delta>0. (47)

The same equivalence holds at any one positive budget. Minimizing Gt,sG_{t,s} therefore also maximizes the radius for every positive budget. For a normalized budget K¯β≤δ¯\overline{K}_{\beta}\leq\bar{\delta}, the radius is 2​D​δ¯/Gt,s\sqrt{2D\bar{\delta}}/G_{t,s}, so the optimum is unchanged at fixed DD. At zero budget, every candidate permits only the zero update.

A.3 Geometry-Optimal Transition

A.3.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Write A=t⁡(1−s)>0A=t(1-s)>0 and B=1−t≥0B=1-t\geq 0. For 0≤β<s0\leq\beta<s, A−B​β≥A−B​s=t−s>0A-B\beta\geq A-Bs=t-s>0, so

For t<1t<1, the derivative changes sign from negative to positive at β⋆=B​s2/A\beta^{\star}=Bs^{2}/A. This point lies in the domain because β⋆/s=s⁡(1−t)/(t⁡(1−s))<1\beta^{\star}/s=s(1-t)/(t(1-s))<1, which is equivalent to s<ts<t. For t=1t=1, B=0B=0 and the derivative is strictly positive for β>0\beta>0, so the unique minimum is the boundary point β⋆=0\beta^{\star}=0. In both cases α⋆=s2−(β⋆)2\alpha^{\star}=\sqrt{s^{2}-(\beta^{\star})^{2}} is uniquely determined by positivity and the coefficient constraint. Extending the domain to −s<β<s-s<\beta<s leaves the unique minimizer unchanged: A​β−B​s2<0A\beta-Bs^{2}<0 throughout β<0\beta<0.

Substitution yields

(Gt,s⋆)2=A2−B2​s2s2=(A−B​s)​(A+B​s)s2=(t−s)​(t+s−2​t​s)s2.(G_{t,s}^{\star})^{2}=\frac{A^{2}-B^{2}s^{2}}{s^{2}}=\frac{(A-Bs)(A+Bs)}{s^{2}}=\frac{(t-s)(t+s-2ts)}{s^{2}}. (49)

Taking the positive square root proves the stated minimum. Proposition 1 then establishes that these coefficients minimize the conditional KL for every prescribed nonzero velocity-output update. □\square

(Gs+Δ,s⋆)2=2​(1−s)s​Δ+1−2​ss2​Δ2,Gs+Δ,s⋆=2​(1−s)s​Δ+O⁡(Δ3/2).(G_{s+\Delta,s}^{\star})^{2}=\frac{2(1-s)}{s}\Delta+\frac{1-2s}{s^{2}}\Delta^{2},\qquad G_{s+\Delta,s}^{\star}=\sqrt{\frac{2(1-s)}{s}}\sqrt{\Delta}+O(\Delta^{3/2}). (50)

β1,s⋆=0,α1,s⋆=s,G1,s⋆=1−ss.\beta_{1,s}^{\star}=0,\qquad\alpha_{1,s}^{\star}=s,\qquad G_{1,s}^{\star}=\frac{1-s}{s}. (52)

For 0<s<t<10<s<t<1, the one-step SDE-DPM-Solver++ transition with data prediction (Lu et al., 2022) is

st​b​𝒙t+(1−s)​(1−b2)​𝒙^0\displaystyle\frac{s}{t}b\bm{x}_{t}+(1-s)(1-b^{2})\hat{\bm{x}}_{0} =(1−s)​𝒙^0+s​b​ϵ^,\displaystyle=(1-s)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}+sb\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}, (54)
s​b\displaystyle sb =βt,s⋆,s1−b2=αt,s⋆.\displaystyle=\beta_{t,s}^{\star},\qquad s\sqrt{1-b^{2}}=\alpha_{t,s}^{\star}.

Thus the coefficients agree exactly for every velocity prediction, without an oracle assumption. The correspondence extends continuously to t=1t=1 through b=0b=0; the log-SNR itself is not finite at that endpoint.

A Gaussian Markov interpretation.

A related interpretation uses a Gaussian Markov process with the same one-time conditional marginals as the linear probability path. For 0<s<t≤10<s<t\leq 1, define

𝒙s|𝒙0\displaystyle\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{x}_{0} ∼𝒩⁡((1−s)​𝒙0,s2​𝑰),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}((1-s)\bm{x}_{0},s^{2}\bm{I}), (55)
𝒙t|𝒙s\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t}\mid\bm{x}_{s} ∼𝒩(γt,s𝒙s,(t2−γt,s2s2)𝑰),γt,s=1−t1−s.\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\gamma_{t,s}\bm{x}_{s},(t^{2}-\gamma_{t,s}^{2}s^{2})\bm{I}),\qquad\gamma_{t,s}=\frac{1-t}{1-s}.

The innovation variance is positive because t>γt,s​st>\gamma_{t,s}s. The resulting marginal is 𝒙t|𝒙0∼𝒩⁡((1−t)​𝒙0,t2​𝑰)\bm{x}_{t}\mid\bm{x}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}((1-t)\bm{x}_{0},t^{2}\bm{I}). This Markov coupling differs from interpolating with a single shared noise vector at all times; the marginal path alone does not specify the joint law across time.

Gaussian conditioning gives

𝔼[𝒙s∣𝒙t,𝒙0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{x}_{0}] =(1−s)​𝒙0+s2​γt,st2​(𝒙t−(1−t)​𝒙0),\displaystyle=(1-s)\bm{x}_{0}+\frac{s^{2}\gamma_{t,s}}{t^{2}}(\bm{x}_{t}-(1-t)\bm{x}_{0}), (56)
Cov⁡(𝒙s∣𝒙t,𝒙0)\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{x}_{s}\mid\bm{x}_{t},\bm{x}_{0}) =(s2−s4​γt,s2t2)​𝑰.\displaystyle=\left(s^{2}-\frac{s^{4}\gamma_{t,s}^{2}}{t^{2}}\right)\bm{I}.

Replacing 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} by 𝒙^0\hat{\bm{x}}_{0} and substituting 𝒙t−(1−t)​𝒙^0=t​ϵ^\bm{x}_{t}-(1-t)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}=t\hat{\bm{\epsilon}} yields βt,s=s2​γt,s/t=βt,s⋆\beta_{t,s}=s^{2}\gamma_{t,s}/t=\beta_{t,s}^{\star} and αt,s=αt,s⋆\alpha_{t,s}=\alpha_{t,s}^{\star}. This is a plug-in posterior interpretation of the selected transition, rather than a claim that the learned reconstruction gives the true posterior of the data.

A.4 Derivation and Scope of Geometry-Matched Scaling

The weights match two explicit scales of the selected conditional policy. For actions sampled from the current policy, Eq. 33 becomes ∇𝒗​log​qθ=sgn⁡(κt,s⋆)​Gt,s⋆​𝝃\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\theta}=\operatorname{sgn}(\kappa_{t,s}^{\star})G_{t,s}^{\star}\bm{\xi}, where 𝝃∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰)\bm{\xi}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}); the action is held fixed when differentiating. The same identity applies at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}} for recorded rollout actions. Multiplying the score by wpolicy=cgeo/Gt,s⋆w^{\mathrm{policy}}=c_{\mathrm{geo}}/G_{t,s}^{\star} makes this explicit coefficient have magnitude cgeoc_{\mathrm{geo}}.

For a stored old-policy action evaluated after the model changes, the standardized residual is instead

𝝃θ=𝝃old−κt,s⋆αt,s⋆​Δ​𝒗,∇𝒗​log​qθ=κt,s⋆αt,s⋆​𝝃old−(Gt,s⋆)2​Δ​𝒗.\bm{\xi}_{\theta}=\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{old}}-\frac{\kappa_{t,s}^{\star}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{\star}}\Delta\bm{v},\qquad\nabla_{\bm{v}}\log q_{\theta}=\frac{\kappa_{t,s}^{\star}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{\star}}\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{old}}-(G_{t,s}^{\star})^{2}\Delta\bm{v}. (57)

Here 𝝃old\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{old}} is standard Gaussian under the old policy. Consequently, canceling the leading coefficient does not remove all geometry dependence of later optimization gradients. Advantages, the likelihood ratio, clipping, the model Jacobian, and the optimizer further affect the parameter update.

For the reference term, both policies use the selected coefficients, so

DKL(qθ∥qref)=12(Gt,s⋆)2∥𝒗θ−𝒗ref∥22,∇𝒗θ2DKL=(Gt,s⋆)2𝑰.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\theta}\|q_{\mathrm{ref}})=\frac{1}{2}(G_{t,s}^{\star})^{2}\|\bm{v}_{\theta}-\bm{v}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\nabla_{\bm{v}_{\theta}}^{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}=(G_{t,s}^{\star})^{2}\bm{I}. (58)

The weight wKL=(cgeo/Gt,s⋆)2w^{\mathrm{KL}}=(c_{\mathrm{geo}}/G_{t,s}^{\star})^{2} maps this curvature to cgeo2​𝑰c_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}\bm{I}. The same covariance also makes the KL symmetric, although its reference-regularization role differs from the updated-to-old conditional KL used for policy selection.

Dimension averaging introduces a factor 1/D1/D into both the log-density score and the reference KL. With the same weights, their matched explicit scales become cgeo/Dc_{\mathrm{geo}}/D and cgeo2/Dc_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}/D, respectively. Thus the relative transition-wise weights are unchanged at fixed DD. This does not turn the averaged log-density into the log of a normalized joint policy, or make its score outer product equal to the curvature of the averaged KL.

Estimator scale and signal-to-noise ratio.

At a fixed state, timestep pair, and latent dimension, with θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, an unclipped negative policy-surrogate gradient has the form 𝒈^β=(Gβ/D)​𝒀β\widehat{\bm{g}}_{\beta}=(G_{\beta}/D)\bm{Y}_{\beta}, where 𝒀β=Aβ​𝑱⊤​𝝃\bm{Y}_{\beta}=A_{\beta}\bm{J}^{\top}\bm{\xi} and 𝑱=∂𝒗/∂θ\bm{J}=\partial\bm{v}/\partial\theta. For nonzero variance, the explicit factor cancels from ‖𝔼​𝒈^β‖2/tr⁡Cov⁡(𝒈^β)\|\mathbb{E}\widehat{\bm{g}}_{\beta}\|_{2}/\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\bm{g}}_{\beta})}. The action–advantage distribution nevertheless depends on the policy, so this cancellation establishes neither equality nor an ordering of signal-to-noise ratios across coefficient choices. For example, in one dimension with x=μ+α​ξx=\mu+\alpha\xi, reward R⁡(x)=xR(x)=x, and its exact mean as baseline, A=α​ξA=\alpha\xi and the reward-gradient estimator is κ​ξ2\kappa\xi^{2}; its signal-to-noise ratio is 1/21/\sqrt{2} for every α>0\alpha>0. Thus increasing noise need not increase estimator signal-to-noise ratio.

The global matching multiplier.

Writing P=𝔼⁡[ℓ¯clip/G⋆]P=\mathbb{E}[\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{clip}}/G^{\star}] and K=𝔼⁡[D¯KL/(G⋆)2]K=\mathbb{E}[\overline{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}/(G^{\star})^{2}] gives ℒ⁡(c,λ)=c​P+λ​c2​K\mathcal{L}(c,\lambda)=cP+\lambda c^{2}K and ℒ⁡(a​c,λ/a)=a​ℒ​(c,λ)\mathcal{L}(ac,\lambda/a)=a\mathcal{L}(c,\lambda) for a>0a>0. Thus cc affects the relative reference penalty and an overall loss scale. Plain SGD offsets the latter by dividing the learning rate by aa. AdamW instead cancels uniform gradient scaling at the same learning rate in the zero-ϵ\epsilon, unclipped limit with zero-initialized moments. Finite optimizer ϵ\epsilon and a fixed gradient-clipping threshold can prevent exact equivalence. The multiplier does not change the sampling policy or its conditional KL cost for a prescribed velocity update.

Appendix B Experimental Details

Table 6 lists the training hyperparameters for the GRPO-based experiments.

Flow-GRPO uses noise level 0.70.7 for main image comparisons and 0.30.3 for video, and caps the injected transition standard deviation at 0.450.45 (Appendix A.1). Flow-CPS uses ϕ=0.7\phi=0.7 for the main image comparisons and ϕ=0.3\phi=0.3 for video; the image single-reward scan also tests 0.30.3, 0.50.5, and 1.01.0. Flow-CPS and Geo-FSRL both use cgeo=0.5c_{\mathrm{geo}}=0.5 in their matched weights. The policy-only ablation sets wpolicy=1w^{\mathrm{policy}}=1 and retains each method’s wKLw^{\mathrm{KL}}.

For each reward, we subtract the prompt-group mean and divide by the largest prompt-group standard deviation in the collected rollout batch, with a stabilizer of 10−410^{-4}. In multi-reward training, the resulting reward-specific advantages are summed with equal weights and clipped to [−5,5][-5,5].

Reported rewards.

For each task, the curves and tabulated automatic reward scores are computed on the same fixed set of 256 validation prompts, shared across methods and held out from training. Curve horizontal axes count optimizer updates. The image CLIP score uses CLIP ViT-L/14 matching logits divided by 30; it is a scaled similarity and need not lie in [0,1][0,1]. For video, HPSv3-General averages frame scores using the generic prompt “A high-quality image.” HPSv3-Percentile uses the video caption and averages the top 30% of frame scores. For VideoAlign-MQ, we increase the number of sampled frames per second to improve stability, similar to previous work (Xue et al., 2025). the All reported automatic metrics are also optimized during training; the human comparison reports descriptive preferences, with shared images and evaluators across ratings.

B.1 Timestep Schedule and Coefficients

Wan uses t=5​u/(1+4​u)t=5u/(1+4u) for u∈{1,3/4,1/2,1/4,0}u\in\{1,3/4,1/2,1/4,0\}, giving (1,0.9375,0.833333​…,0.625,0)(1,0.9375,0.833333\ldots,0.625,0) for both training and evaluation. Qwen uses four steps from the scheduler saved with its Lightning checkpoint. The last transition to s=0s=0 is deterministic and is excluded from policy optimization. Table 7 compares the coefficients on the Wan grid.

Video comparisons use ϕ=0.3\phi=0.3 for greater geometric separation from the optimum, whose ϕ⋆\phi^{\star} values are approximately (1,0.783653,0.783653)(1,0.783653,0.783653). With ϕ=0.7\phi=0.7, GG is only 1.03%1.03\% above G⋆G^{\star} at the two interior-source transitions and 12.23%12.23\% above at the first. This analytic comparison does not establish a reward ordering between Flow-CPS settings.

B.2 Training Algorithm

Sampling arrangement.

For each rollout batch, we select one non-terminal transition index k∈{0,…,K−2}k\in\{0,\ldots,K-2\} and use the stochastic policy only at that step. All other steps use deterministic Euler updates with the frozen sampling model θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}}. Only the selected transition contributes to the loss, with its trajectory’s terminal reward determining the advantage; no gradient is propagated through the rollout. The index cycles across rollout batches, and the recorded transitions are shuffled before optimization. The expectation in Eq. 18 is over these rollout batches, prompts, and group trajectories. At inference, the updated velocity model uses the original deterministic few-step solver.

Appendix C Additional Ablation Results

Figure 3 gives the validation curves for Table 3, with KL weighting retained throughout. The Geo-FSRL–Flow-CPS score difference changes from −0.08-0.08 without policy weighting to +0.15+0.15 with matched weighting, an observed interaction contrast of 0.230.23. The matched comparison changes both the coefficients and their corresponding numerical weights. It therefore evaluates their combination rather than isolating coefficient changes under fixed numerical weights; no cross-seed inference is made from this single-run contrast.

The coefficient scan compares globally fixed splits with the transition-wise rule, as discussed in Section 3 and the image experiments. The reported reward curves do not measure clipping frequency or log-ratio variance, so they do not establish which mechanism mediates the observed gains.

Conditional gradient-scale comparison.

Fix the conditioning state and timestep pair (t,s)(t,s), and compare the two policies at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, where the ratio is one and clipping is inactive. Let 𝑱=∂𝒗θ/∂θ\bm{J}=\partial\bm{v}_{\theta}/\partial\theta be the velocity-model Jacobian. For method m∈{CPS,Geo}m\in\{\mathrm{CPS},\mathrm{Geo}\}, the gradient of the negative, dimension-averaged policy surrogate without policy reweighting is

𝒈policy(m)=−AD​κt,s(m)αt,s(m)​𝑱⊤​𝝃=A​Gt,s(m)D​𝑱⊤​𝝃,\bm{g}_{\mathrm{policy}}^{(m)}=-\frac{A}{D}\frac{\kappa_{t,s}^{(m)}}{\alpha_{t,s}^{(m)}}\bm{J}^{\top}\bm{\xi}=\frac{AG_{t,s}^{(m)}}{D}\bm{J}^{\top}\bm{\xi}, (59)

where the action and advantage are held fixed when differentiating, 𝝃\bm{\xi} is the standardized residual under the old policy, and the last equality uses κt,s(m)<0\kappa_{t,s}^{(m)}<0. Holding AA, 𝝃\bm{\xi}, 𝑱\bm{J}, and DD fixed across the two policies therefore gives

𝒈policy(CPS)=Gt,sCPSGt,s⋆​𝒈policy(Geo).\bm{g}_{\mathrm{policy}}^{(\mathrm{CPS})}=\frac{G_{t,s}^{\mathrm{CPS}}}{G_{t,s}^{\star}}\bm{g}_{\mathrm{policy}}^{(\mathrm{Geo})}. (60)

Since Gt,sCPS≥Gt,s⋆G_{t,s}^{\mathrm{CPS}}\geq G_{t,s}^{\star}, the Flow-CPS gradient norm is no smaller than that of Geo-FSRL in this controlled comparison; the inequality is strict when the geometry factors differ and the common gradient is nonzero. This statement concerns a fixed transition. Matching training hyperparameters alone does not hold the sampled advantages, residuals, or model Jacobians fixed, and the statement does not order the norm of a batch gradient mixing different transitions.

Relation to the reward ordering.

For either policy, applying its matched KL weight gives

wt,sKL​D¯KL=cgeo22​D​‖𝒗θ−𝒗ref‖22.w_{t,s}^{\mathrm{KL}}\overline{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{geo}}^{2}}{2D}\|\bm{v}_{\theta}-\bm{v}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}. (61)

Thus, retaining KL reweighting while removing policy reweighting normalizes the reference-penalty curvature in velocity space but leaves Gt,sG_{t,s} in the policy gradient. With the other gradient factors controlled, Flow-CPS’s larger geometry factor increases the policy-gradient scale relative to this matched regularizer. This is a conditional scale explanation compatible with its slightly higher unweighted reward, rather than a measured attribution of that difference. Appendix A.4 details how full updates depend on the coefficients and optimizer. The ablation evaluates cross-timestep balancing together with changes in the overall policy-to-regularization scale.
